message.content:
The largest planet that astronomers have confirmed so far is **HD 100546 b**.  
It orbits the young star HD 100546 (about 320 light‑years away in the constellation Musca) and has a radius of roughly **2.5 – 3 times that of Jupiter** (≈ 200,000 km). Its mass is estimated at about 10–20 Jupiter masses, placing it right on the boundary between giant planets and brown dwarfs.

> **Why it’s the biggest known**  
> * HD 100546 b was first imaged in 2013 and has been studied extensively with the VLT and other telescopes.  
> * Its size and mass are larger than any other confirmed exoplanet to date.  
> * While some objects classified as “planets” are actually brown dwarfs (e.g., HD 106906 b), HD 100546 b is still considered a planet because it formed in a protoplanetary disk rather than through cloud collapse.

> **What could be even bigger?**  
> The universe is vast, and new surveys (e.g., TESS, PLATO, JWST) are constantly discovering larger exoplanets. Some candidates—especially those near the deuterium‑burning limit (~13 M_J)—might turn out to be even larger once their masses and radii are measured more precisely. Until such measurements are confirmed, HD 100546 b remains the record holder.

So, if you’re looking for the biggest planet we know of, it’s HD 100546 b. Keep an eye on future discoveries; the cosmic “biggest” list can change as new data come in!
